title: Alcohol use and burden for 195 countries and territories, 1990–2016: A systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2016

claims.statement: In the world's population in 2020, alcohol drinking compared with a counterfactual in which no one had ever drunk (lifetime abstention) is estimated by one modelling study to account for 741,300 new cancer cases (95% uncertainty interval 558,500–951,200), about 4 in every 100 new cancers (4.1%, 3.1%–5.3%; non-melanoma skin cancer excluded): about 6 in 100 new cancers in men (568,700 cases; 6.1%) and 2 in 100 in women (172,600; 2.0%) (Rumgay et al., 2021; no funding, no competing interests declared). The model counts only the cancers that the International Agency for Research on Cancer judges to be caused by alcohol: oesophagus (squamous cell carcinoma only) 189,700 cases, 31.6% of all oesophageal cancers; liver (hepatocellular carcinoma only) 154,700, 17.3%; female breast 98,300, 4.4%; colon 91,500, 8.1%; lip and oral cavity 74,900, 20.2%; rectum 65,100, 9.0%; pharynx 39,400, 22.0%; and larynx 27,600, 15.0%. It attributes 346,400 cases (46.7%) to drinking more than 60 g of ethanol a day, 291,800 (39.4%) to 20–60 g and 103,100 (13.9%; interval 82,600–207,200) to less than 20 g a day (up to about two drinks), including 41,300 (35,400–145,800) to drinking up to 10 g a day, of which 24,600 were in women, 14.3% of women's alcohol-attributed cancers. These are model estimates, not counts of people whose cancer was traced to drinking: they combine drinking estimated from 2010 sales and surveys, assumed to act 10 years later, with relative-risk curves for current drinking from World Cancer Research Fund reviews of observational studies, applied in the same way to every country; former drinkers carry no extra risk in the main analysis; the uncertainty intervals carry only the uncertainty in drinking and in the relative risks, leave out that in cancer incidence, the 10-year delay and the model's structure, and are lopsided for the low-intake figures; and the hepatocellular share behind the liver figure comes from unpublished estimates. Adding stomach and pancreatic cancer raised the total to 808,700, and counting former drinking raised it to 925,900, though the increment the paper gives for this (135,000) does not match its own totals. Earlier global estimates cited by the paper, for other years and with other choices, were 5.5% of new cancers in 2012 and 4.8% to 4.9% of cancer deaths in 2016 and 2019; an earlier model by an overlapping team estimated 487 thousand cancer deaths caused by alcohol in 2004 (377 thousand in men, 111 thousand in women; no uncertainty intervals; Rehm et al., 2009); and in the Global Burden of Disease 2016 study, cancers made up 27.1% of the deaths attributed to alcohol in women aged 50 and older and 18.9% in men (Griswold et al., 2018). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.

In people taking part in the same 572 case–control and cohort studies (Bagnardi et al., 2015), light drinking (up to 12.5 g of ethanol a day on average, one drink or less as the review defines it) compared with not drinking (nondrinkers, combined with occasional drinkers in 24% of the studies; former drinkers not separated) is associated with slightly more of some cancers and slightly fewer of others, with no absolute risks reported: pooled relative risks of 1.13 (95% CI 1.00–1.26) for cancers of the mouth and pharynx (52 studies), 1.26 (1.06–1.50) for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (54 studies), 1.04 (1.01–1.07) for female breast cancer (115 studies, editors' count) and 1.04 (1.01–1.08) for prostate cancer; no clear difference for cancers of the colon and rectum (0.99, 0.95–1.04), liver (1.00, 0.85–1.18) or larynx (0.87, 0.68–1.11); and lower figures for lung cancer (0.84, 0.79–0.88), oesophageal adenocarcinoma with gastric cardia (0.86, 0.76–0.98), cancers of the kidney (0.92, 0.86–0.99) and thyroid (0.81, 0.74–0.88), and both kinds of lymphoma (Hodgkin's 0.73, 0.59–0.89; non-Hodgkin's 0.88, 0.80–0.97). Differences this small can be produced or hidden by people who drink more reporting less, which the authors say may partly or largely explain the light-drinking associations, by smoking and other differences (only 297 of the 572 studies reported adjusted estimates), and by former or occasional drinkers among the comparison group; the raised figures for the mouth and pharynx and the oesophagus were statistically clear only in Asian studies (1.33 and 1.54), and the lower lung and oesophageal adenocarcinoma figures appear in the review's figure but not in its text. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 study, drawing on an overlapping set of studies, fitted risk curves that rise with intake for every cancer (Griswold et al., 2018), and a model of cancers in 2020 attributes 41,300 new cases worldwide (95% uncertainty interval 35,400–145,800) to drinking up to 10 g a day, against lifetime abstention (Rumgay et al., 2021); both depend on the shape of the risk curves at low intake, which is what these studies leave uncertain. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: Bagnardi et al. 2015, light drinking against nondrinkers or occasional drinkers (pooled RR, 95% CI; I²): mouth and pharynx 1.13 (1.00–1.26; 26%); oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 1.26 (1.06–1.50; 68%); female breast 1.04 (1.01–1.07; 63%); prostate 1.04 (1.01–1.08); colon and rectum 0.99 (0.95–1.04); liver 1.00 (0.85–1.18); larynx 0.87 (0.68–1.11); lung 0.84 (0.79–0.88); oesophageal adenocarcinoma and gastric cardia 0.86 (0.76–0.98); kidney 0.92 (0.86–0.99); thyroid 0.81 (0.74–0.88); Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.73 (0.59–0.89); non-Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.88 (0.80–0.97). Asian studies only: mouth and pharynx 1.33 (1.06–1.68; 7 studies), oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 1.54 (1.18–2.00; 11 studies). Rumgay et al. 2021 (model): 41,300 (35,400–145,800) new cancers in 2020 attributed to intake up to 10 g a day against lifetime abstention.

claims.statement: In people taking part in 572 case–control and cohort studies published from 1956 to 2012 (486,538 people with cancer; 41% of the studies from North America, 32% from Europe and 18% from Asia), drinking more than 12.5 g of ethanol a day on average (more than one drink as the review defines it) compared with not drinking (nondrinkers, combined with occasional drinkers in 24% of the studies; former drinkers were not separated) is associated with more cancers of the mouth and pharynx, the oesophagus (squamous cell carcinoma only), the larynx, the colon and rectum and the female breast, and, at heavy drinking, of the liver, with the relative risk rising with the amount (Bagnardi et al., 2015; funded by Italian cancer-research charities, no conflicts declared). The review reports no absolute risks, so its ratios cannot be turned into numbers out of 100. For heavy drinking (above 50 g a day, more than four drinks) the pooled relative risks were 5.13 (95% CI 4.31–6.10) for the mouth and pharynx, 4.95 (3.86–6.34) for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, 2.65 (2.19–3.19) for the larynx, 2.07 (1.66–2.58) for the liver, 1.61 (1.33–1.94) for the breast (from 11 of the 118 breast studies, editors' count) and 1.44 (1.25–1.65) for the colon and rectum; for moderate drinking (above 12.5 and up to 50 g a day) they were 1.83 (1.62–2.07), 2.23 (1.87–2.65), 1.44 (1.25–1.66), 1.08 (0.97–1.20, no clear difference), 1.23 (1.19–1.28) and 1.17 (1.11–1.24). Heavy drinking was also associated with cancers of the stomach (1.21, 1.07–1.36), pancreas (1.19, 1.11–1.28), lung (1.15, 1.02–1.30) and gallbladder (2.64, 1.62–4.30; 8 studies), and moderate drinking with small increases in prostate cancer (1.06, 1.01–1.11) and melanoma (1.20, 1.03–1.41), clear only in North American studies; there was no clear association with oesophageal adenocarcinoma or with cancers of the small intestine, cervix, endometrium, ovary, bladder or brain; and cancers of the kidney and thyroid and both kinds of lymphoma were less common in people who drank (for example non-Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.75, 0.64–0.88, at heavy drinking): for the lymphomas the authors suggest that people stop or cut down when early symptoms start, while they read the kidney result both as protection and, in their conclusion, as no association. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 study, whose own review of studies overlaps with this one, fitted risk curves that rise with intake for every cancer it included (Griswold et al., 2018). Results varied widely between studies (I² up to 91%), only 297 of the 572 studies reported adjusted estimates, so differences in smoking and other habits were often not taken into account, case–control studies gave stronger associations than cohort studies at some sites (heavy drinking and liver cancer 2.79 against 1.12; larynx 2.81 against 1.12), and the review neither appraised the studies nor tested for publication bias. That alcohol causes cancer at these sites is the judgment of the International Agency for Research on Cancer, whose list a 2021 cancer-burden model used (Rumgay et al., 2021); this pooling of observational studies cannot show it by itself. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Bagnardi et al. 2015, pooled relative risks (random effects; 95% CI) against nondrinkers or occasional drinkers, moderate then heavy drinking: mouth and pharynx 1.83 (1.62–2.07), 5.13 (4.31–6.10; I² 72%, 77%); oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 2.23 (1.87–2.65), 4.95 (3.86–6.34; I² 85%, 91%); larynx 1.44 (1.25–1.66), 2.65 (2.19–3.19); colon and rectum 1.17 (1.11–1.24), 1.44 (1.25–1.65); liver 1.08 (0.97–1.20), 2.07 (1.66–2.58); female breast 1.23 (1.19–1.28), 1.61 (1.33–1.94; I² 54%, 10%; heavy from 11 studies, editors' count); heavy only: stomach 1.21 (1.07–1.36), pancreas 1.19 (1.11–1.28), lung 1.15 (1.02–1.30), gallbladder 2.64 (1.62–4.30); moderate: prostate 1.06 (1.01–1.11), melanoma 1.20 (1.03–1.41); inverse: kidney moderate 0.79 (0.72–0.86), thyroid moderate 0.81 (0.71–0.94), Hodgkin's lymphoma heavy 0.63 (0.41–0.97), non-Hodgkin's lymphoma heavy 0.75 (0.64–0.88). By design, heavy drinking: mouth and pharynx 5.34 (4.46–6.39; 35 case–control studies) against 3.13 (1.59–6.19; 3 cohort studies); liver 2.79 (2.00–3.87; 24 case–control) against 1.12 (1.02–1.23; 7 cohort); larynx 2.81 (2.33–3.39) against 1.12 (0.75–1.67; 3 cohort). No absolute risks reported.

claims.statement: In the world's population, alcohol use compared with no alcohol use is estimated by two global models to account for about 2.3 million (2004, after subtracting deaths the model counted as prevented; editors' rounding) to 2.8 million (2016) deaths a year. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 study estimated 2.8 million deaths in 2016 (95% uncertainty interval 2.4–3.3 million), 2.2% of age-standardised deaths in women and 6.8% in men, about 2 and 7 in every 100; it ranked alcohol seventh among risk factors overall and first at ages 15 to 49, where 3.8% of women's and 12.2% of men's deaths were attributed to it, the leading causes being tuberculosis, road injuries and self-harm (Griswold et al., 2018; funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation). A WHO comparative risk assessment for 2004 estimated 2482 thousand deaths caused by alcohol, less 227 thousand deaths it modelled as prevented (215 thousand from heart and blood-vessel disease, 12 thousand from diabetes), leaving 2255 thousand, 3.8 in every 100 deaths worldwide (6.3 in 100 deaths of men and 1.1 in 100 of women) and 5.3 in 100 deaths before the age of 60; the deaths caused were mainly from unintentional injuries (666 thousand), heart and blood-vessel disease (545 thousand), cancer (487 thousand), liver cirrhosis (373 thousand) and intentional injuries (272 thousand) (Rehm et al., 2009; the underlying assessments supported by WHO and the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health; no conflicts declared). These are model estimates, not counted deaths: they combine estimated drinking (sales data, estimates of unrecorded alcohol, which is more than a quarter of the world's drinking, and surveys) with relative-risk curves from observational studies, mostly of middle-class cohorts in high-income countries, applied to every population. The 2004 estimate has no uncertainty intervals, and the 2016 paper does not say that its intervals include uncertainty from the model's structure or from bias in the underlying studies; the net figures depend on protective heart and diabetes estimates at low intake, which the 2004 authors call controversial; the 2016 figure is counted against a minimum-risk level of zero drinks a day, whose interval reached 0.8 drinks (10 g each) a day and which moved to about half a drink a day when the same group updated its weights (0.534, 0–1.00; Bryazka et al., 2022); the 2016 authors expect their figures to be underestimates, because drinking patterns, harm to others from violence and people under 15 were left out; and the two estimates used different methods and inputs, so the difference between them is not a trend. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
claims.magnitude: Griswold et al. 2018 (GBD 2016; 95% uncertainty intervals): 2.8 million (2.4–3.3) deaths in 2016; 2.2% (1.5–3.0) of age-standardised female and 6.8% (5.8–8.0) of male deaths; 1.6% (1.4–2.0) and 6.0% (5.4–6.7) of DALYs; ages 15–49: 3.8% (3.2–4.3) of female and 12.2% (10.8–13.6) of male deaths; leading attributable causes at 15–49: tuberculosis 1.4% (1.0–1.7), road injuries 1.2% (0.7–1.9) and self-harm 1.1% (0.6–1.5) of total deaths; minimum-risk level 0 (0.0–0.8) standard drinks of 10 g a day. Rehm et al. 2009 (WHO comparative risk assessment, 2004; thousands; no intervals): caused 2482 (men 2039, women 443); prevented 227 (cardiovascular 215, diabetes 12); net 2255 (men 1944, women 311) of 58 738 deaths, 3.8% (men 6.3%, women 1.1%); under age 60, 5.3% (men 7.9%, women 1.9%); deaths caused by cause: unintentional injuries 666, cardiovascular 545, cancer 487, cirrhosis 373, intentional injuries 272, neuropsychiatric 135, perinatal 3. Bryazka et al. 2022: global minimum-risk level 0.534 (0–1.00) drinks a day with the GBD 2016 curves and GBD 2020 weights.

claims.statement: In adults without heart disease when they joined prospective cohort studies, mostly in high-income countries, drinking a little compared with not drinking is associated with less coronary heart disease, but how much less depends on who is counted as not drinking, and no paper read gives absolute risks, so the ratios cannot be turned into numbers out of 100. Against non-drinkers as each study defined them (in most studies people not drinking at the start, including former drinkers), people who drank had pooled relative risks of 0.71 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.77) for new coronary heart disease (29 studies) and 0.75 (0.68 to 0.81) for coronary death (31 studies); at 2.5 to 14.9 g of ethanol a day (up to about one drink, counted as 12.5 g where a study gave no grams) the figures were 0.75 (0.65 to 0.88) and 0.79 (0.73 to 0.86), below 2.5 g a day 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06) and 0.92 (0.80 to 1.06), and at every higher intake, up to more than 60 g a day, 0.66 to 0.79; 8 of the 84 cohort reports gave only unadjusted estimates (Ronksley et al., 2011). In the 7 to 9 studies that compared with lifetime abstainers the figures were similar (0.73, 0.61 to 0.88; 0.75, 0.66 to 0.85), and former drinkers had more coronary deaths (1.31, 1.02 to 1.68; against non-drinkers in the paper's table, against people who drank in its text). A review that compared only with lifetime abstainers and kept men, women, deaths and new cases apart (Roerecke & Rehm, 2012; 24 studies) found lower point estimates at about one drink of 12 g a day in all four groups, but men's coronary deaths were not clearly lower at about one or two drinks a day (0.89, 0.79 to 1.00; 0.86, 0.73 to 1.02) and women's were not lower at about two drinks (1.03, 0.84 to 1.27); with all 44 studies, including those that combined men and women or deaths and new cases, every estimate at about one to three drinks a day was lower (0.62 to 0.81), and occasional drinking (less than weekly, or under 2.5 g a day) was not associated with coronary risk in any group. Of 23 conditions in the GBD 2016 curves fitted to 592 studies, only ischaemic heart disease showed a significant dip, lowest at 0.83 drinks of 10 g a day in men (relative risk 0.86, 95% uncertainty interval 0.80 to 0.96) and 0.92 in women (0.82, 0.72 to 0.95). Self-reported drinking showed the same dip in Chinese men (Millwood et al., 2019) and in UK Biobank, where allowing for smoking, body mass index, physical activity, cooked vegetable and red meat intake and self-rated health removed the statistically clear difference at moderate intake (more than 8.4 to 15.4 US drinks of 14 g a week) and, read approximately from the paper's figure, reduced but did not remove it at light intake (Biddinger et al., 2022). Whether alcohol causes the lower risk is disputed: in the same team's earlier review, cited second-hand, former drinkers had more coronary deaths than lifetime abstainers (men 1.25, women 1.54), and in men drinking 60 g a day or more the lower risk seen against current non-drinkers (0.75, 0.63 to 0.89) was not seen against lifetime abstainers (1.00, 0.74 to 1.36; Roerecke & Rehm, 2014); genetic studies do not find the lower risk (see the answer on gene studies). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Ronksley et al. 2011 (prospective cohorts to September 2009; against non-drinkers as each study defined them, mostly current non-drinkers including former drinkers; each study's most-adjusted estimate, unadjusted for 8 of 84): any drinking, incident CHD RR 0.71 (0.66–0.77; 29 studies), CHD mortality 0.75 (0.68–0.81; 31), CVD mortality 0.75 (0.70–0.80; 21); I² 72.2%. By intake (under 2.5, 2.5–14.9, 15–29.9, 30–60, over 60 g/day): incident CHD 0.96 (0.86–1.06), 0.75 (0.65–0.88), 0.66 (0.59–0.75), 0.67 (0.56–0.79), 0.76 (0.52–1.09); CHD mortality 0.92 (0.80–1.06), 0.79 (0.73–0.86), 0.79 (0.71–0.88), 0.77 (0.72–0.83), 0.75 (0.63–0.89). Against lifetime abstainers: incident CHD 0.73 (0.61–0.88; 9 studies), CHD mortality 0.75 (0.66–0.85; 7), CVD mortality 0.82 (0.78–0.86; 9). Former drinkers (against non-drinkers by the table, against drinkers by the text): CHD mortality 1.31 (1.02–1.68), CVD mortality 1.48 (1.23–1.79), incident CHD 1.10 (0.91–1.33). Roerecke & Rehm 2012 (44 studies to April 2010; against lifetime abstainers; former drinkers excluded and mortality corrected for them): fully stratified studies at 2.5–11.99, 12–23.99, 24–35.99 g/day, men's IHD mortality 0.89 (0.79–1.00), 0.86 (0.73–1.02), 0.78 (0.63–0.97); men's morbidity 0.77 (0.65–0.92), 0.75 (0.64–0.88), 0.74 (0.53–1.02); women's mortality 0.84 (0.74–0.96), 1.03 (0.84–1.27), 0.89 (0.57–1.40); women's morbidity 0.54 (0.45–0.65), 0.61 (0.38–0.99), 0.40 (0.14–1.13); occasional drinking 0.82 to 0.98, none significant; all 44 studies 0.62 to 0.81, every interval excluding 1 (occasional 0.87 to 0.97, none significant); I² up to 84%. GBD 2016 (592 studies; against each study's non-drinking category, adjusted for former drinkers in it): IHD minimum RR 0.86 (95% UI 0.80–0.96) in men at 0.83 and 0.82 (0.72–0.95) in women at 0.92 standard drinks (10 g) a day; no significant dip for any other of 23 outcomes. UK Biobank (Biddinger et al. 2022): J- or U-shaped conventional associations; the moderate-intake difference for coronary artery disease not significant after six lifestyle factors (no values printed). China Kadoorie Biobank men (Millwood et al. 2019): conventional U shape for heart attack and CHD (no values printed for non-drinkers). Second-hand (Roerecke & Rehm 2014): former drinkers against lifetime abstainers, IHD mortality men 1.25 (1.15–1.36), women 1.54 (1.17–2.03); men drinking 60 g/day or more, IHD mortality 1.00 (0.74–1.36) against lifetime abstainers, against Ronksley et al.'s 0.75 (0.63–0.89) against current non-drinkers above 60 g/day. No absolute risks in any paper read.

claims.statement: In people averaging less than 30 g of ethanol a day, in seven observational studies pooled by one team, drinking heavily on some occasions compared with drinking the same average amount without such occasions is associated with a higher risk of ischaemic heart disease (deaths and new cases combined); no absolute risks are given. Against lifetime abstainers, people without heavy drinking occasions had a pooled relative risk of 0.64 (95% CI as printed 0.53 to 0.71, an interval that does not fit its point estimate on the log scale, so one figure is probably misprinted; editors' calculation) and people with them 1.12 (0.91 to 1.37), that is, no lower risk than lifetime abstainers; the ratio between the two groups was 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25) (Roerecke & Rehm, 2014). The same team's earlier review, cited second-hand, gave 1.45 (1.24 to 1.70) for people with irregular heavy drinking occasions against people who drank without them. The article does not say what counted as a heavy drinking occasion, which seven studies were pooled or how many people and events they included (all only in a supplement not read); all seven adjusted for age and smoking, one author searched for and extracted the studies, and their risk of bias was not assessed. The review of average intake against lifetime abstainers and the GBD 2016 model did not take drinking pattern into account, and genetic variants that lower average intake also lower heavy drinking (odds of binge drinking 0.78, 0.73 to 0.84, in carriers of the ADH1B variant; Holmes et al., 2014), so two critiques argue that the genetic studies may partly reflect heavy drinking days rather than average amount (Roerecke & Rehm, 2014; Mukamal et al., 2020). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
claims.magnitude: Roerecke & Rehm 2014 (seven studies; against lifetime abstainers; ischaemic heart disease mortality and morbidity combined; most-adjusted estimates, all adjusted for age and smoking): average under 30 g/day without heavy drinking occasions RR 0.64 (0.53–0.71 as printed; geometric midpoint of that interval 0.61, editors' calculation), I² 10%, Egger P = 0.35; with heavy drinking occasions 1.12 (0.91–1.37), I² 0%, Egger P = 0.58; ratio with against without 1.75 (1.36–2.25), equal to 1.12/0.64 (editors' arithmetic), method of its interval not described. Roerecke & Rehm 2010, as cited by Roerecke & Rehm 2012: RR 1.45 (1.24–1.70), drinkers with irregular heavy drinking occasions against drinkers without them. Holmes et al. 2014: ADH1B intake-lowering variant, binge drinking OR 0.78 (0.73–0.84) and 17.2% fewer UK units a week. No absolute risks, numbers of participants or events, or definition of a heavy drinking occasion in the article.

claims.statement: In adults followed in prospective cohort studies of drinking and death (published 1981 to 2021, mostly from North America, Europe and Australia), drinking a little (about 1.3 to 25 g of ethanol a day, from one 10-g drink a week to about two drinks a day) compared with not drinking: the evidence is insufficient to say whether it changes the risk of dying from any cause, and the question is disputed. Against non-drinkers as each study defined them, who in most studies included people who had stopped drinking or drank occasionally, people who drank a little died at lower rates: in a 2006 pooled analysis of 34 cohorts (1,015,835 people, 94,533 deaths) the death rate was lowest at 6 g a day, about half a drink (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.83), and stayed lower up to 42 g a day; in 87 and then 107 cohorts (up to 4,838,825 people and 425,564 deaths) the relative risk at 1.3 to 25 g a day was 0.86 (0.83 to 0.90, and 0.83 to 0.88). These analyses give relative risks only, so the difference cannot be given as a number out of 100 (editors' observation). The difference shrinks or disappears as the comparison group is defined more strictly: people who had stopped drinking, some of them because of illness, died at higher rates than abstainers in the main models (relative risks 1.22 to 1.38); against occasional drinkers, people who drank a little had no lower death rate (1.02, 0.95 to 1.10; 0.97, 0.85 to 1.11 after adjustment), while abstainers had a higher one with limited adjustment (1.19, 1.12 to 1.27) but not after adjustment (1.04, 0.94 to 1.16); after adjustment for study characteristics, including how each study defined its non-drinkers, the estimate was 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) in 87 cohorts and 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01) in 107; in the 13 cohorts that compared with people who had never drunk it was 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06); and in the 6 cohorts that did so and had recruited people at a median age of 55 or younger, 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11), against 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89) in 18 older cohorts whose non-drinkers included former and occasional drinkers. Even in 2006, cohorts whose comparison group left out former and light drinkers showed a smaller reduction (16% against 23% at the lowest point) that ended at 30 rather than 52 g a day. The 2016, 2023 and 2024 analyses are by one research group and reuse the same cohorts; the 6-cohort estimate rests on studies the article does not name and allows anything from a 13% lower to an 11% higher death rate (editors' arithmetic); and genetic studies, which avoid the non-drinker comparison, concern heart disease and diabetes rather than deaths from all causes (see the answers on the heart). None of these designs can show whether drinking a little itself makes people live longer or shorter. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Di Castelnuovo et al. 2006 (34 cohorts, 56 curves, 1,015,835 people, 94,533 deaths; fixed-effect; against each study's lowest-intake category): lowest relative risk 0.81 (95% CI 0.80 to 0.83) at 6 g a day, lower mortality significant up to 42 g a day; adjusted at least for age 17% lower (99% CI 15% to 18%) at 6 g, up to 37 g; with light or former drinkers in the reference group 23% (20% to 26%) at 8 g, up to 52 g; without them 16% (14% to 18%) at 5 g, up to 30 g; the same 34 curves 19% (17% to 21%) crude and 16% (14% to 18%) adjusted. Stockwell et al. 2016 (87 cohorts, 3,998,626 people, 367,103 deaths), low volume 1.30 to 24.9 g a day: against study-defined abstainers 0.86 (0.83 to 0.90), occasional 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89), former 1.22 (1.14 to 1.31); against occasional drinkers, low volume 1.02 (0.95 to 1.10), abstainers 1.19 (1.12 to 1.27); with all study-level covariates, low volume 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07), former 1.38 (1.24 to 1.54); six covariates 0.89 (0.84 to 0.94); 13 lifetime-abstainer studies 0.90 (0.76 to 1.06), former 1.31 (1.09 to 1.57); 7 higher-quality studies 0.89 (0.62 to 1.29), 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15) without one influential study. Zhao et al. 2023 (107 cohorts, 4,838,825 people, 425,564 deaths): unadjusted low volume 0.85 (0.81 to 0.88); fully adjusted 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01; P = .07), occasional 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06), former 1.26 (1.12 to 1.42); against occasional drinkers, fully adjusted, low volume 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11), abstainers 1.04 (0.94 to 1.16); I2 above 85.87% in every category. Stockwell et al. 2024 (subgroups of the 107; random study effect): all 107, 0.86 (0.83 to 0.88; 99 studies with low-volume estimates); 6 studies of cohorts recruited at a median age of 55 or younger against lifetime abstainers 0.98 (0.87 to 1.11), 1.10 (0.97 to 1.24) without the random effect; with a 30-day intake measure as well, 5 studies, 1.04 (0.95 to 1.15); older cohorts with both abstainer biases, 18 studies, 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89); one criterion only, 0.88 (0.84 to 0.92; 51 studies) and 0.88 (0.81 to 0.95; 18 studies); editors' calculation of the difference between 0.98 and 0.84, treating the two sets of studies as independent: ratio 1.17 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.34), p of about .03. No absolute death rates by drinking group in any of the four.

claims.statement: In the world's population aged 15 and older, as modelled in two Global Burden of Disease (GBD) analyses, the second an update of the first that keeps 17 of its curves, drinking compared with not drinking is associated with a combined risk of 22 or 23 alcohol-linked diseases and injuries (each weighted by its share of the population's ill health, measured in disability-adjusted life years, DALYs) that is lowest at or near zero for people aged 15 to 39, and at about half a standard drink (10 g of ethanol) a day for people aged 40 and older: these are model estimates resting on relative-risk curves fitted to observational studies of self-reported drinking, and every lowest point above zero comes from lower risks of ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes in those studies (editors' reading of how the models are built), which genetic studies mostly do not find. In GBD 2016 (Griswold et al., 2018), one curve weighted by the world's 2016 disease mix had its lowest point at 0 standard drinks a day (95% uncertainty interval 0 to 0.8 a day; the abstract prints it per week) and rose with intake; of its 23 conditions only ischaemic heart disease had a significant dip (lowest relative risk 0.86 in men at 0.83 drinks a day and 0.82 in women at 0.92), diabetes and ischaemic stroke dipped non-significantly, and the risks of all the others, every cancer among them, rose with intake; in women the lower heart disease and diabetes risks were offset mainly by cancers. In GBD 2020 (Bryazka et al., 2022), with weights from each region's, age group's and sex's own disease mix, the lowest point at ages 15 to 39 was 0 to 0.603 drinks a day across regions (worldwide 0.136 for men and 0.273 for women), and the combined risk was back at a non-drinker's level at 0.249 drinks a day for men and 0.546 for women worldwide (about 2.5 and 5.5 g; editors' arithmetic), injuries, whose risk rose with intake, making up much of the ill health weighed at these ages (66.3% in men, 47.9% in women); at 40 to 64 the lowest point was 0.527 (men) and 0.562 (women) drinks a day and the non-drinker level was reached at 1.69 and 1.82; at 65 and older, 0.636 and 0.656, and 3.19 and 3.51. Differences between women and men were not significant. Worldwide and age-standardised, the 2020 lowest point was 0.511 (0.400 to 0.700) drinks a day, and 0.534 (0 to 1.00) when the 2016 curves were given the 2020 weights, so the move away from zero comes mostly from the weights (editors' reading). The lowest-risk amount is the bottom of an average of many curves for a whole population, not one person's risk and not a risk-free amount; drinking a lot on some days was not modelled, alcohol use disorder, depression, anxiety and dementia were left out of the 2020 curves, and the authors expect that including the last three would lower the amounts. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: GBD 2016 (Griswold et al., 2018; 23 outcomes, 592 studies, 3,992 relative-risk estimates; one curve weighted by global age-standardised 2016 DALY rates, both sexes; standard drink 10 g): lowest point of the weighted curve 0 standard drinks a day (95% UI 0.0 to 0.8 a day; printed per week in the abstract), rising monotonically; ischaemic heart disease lowest relative risk 0.86 (0.80 to 0.96) in men at 0.83 drinks a day and 0.82 (0.72 to 0.95) in women at 0.92; non-significant dips for diabetes and ischaemic stroke; all cancers rising. GBD 2020 (Bryazka et al., 2022; 22 curves, five re-fitted with 71 more studies; weights by region, age, sex and year; TMREL the lowest point, NDE the return to a non-drinker's risk; standard drinks a day): all populations, TMREL 0 (0 to 0) to 1.87 (0.500 to 3.30); ages 15 to 39 across regions TMREL 0 to 0.603 (0.400 to 1.00), NDE 0.002 (0 to 0) to 1.75 (0.698 to 4.30); global males TMREL 0.136 (0 to 0.400), NDE 0.249 (0 to 1.00), females 0.273 (0 to 0.500) and 0.546 (0 to 1.30); ages 40 to 64, males 0.527 (0.400 to 1.00) and 1.69 (0.800 to 3.20), females 0.562 (0.400 to 0.800) and 1.82 (1.00 to 3.10); 65 and older, males 0.636 (0.500 to 1.00) and 3.19 (1.50 to 5.20), females 0.656 (0.500 to 1.00) and 3.51 (1.70 to 5.50); ages 40 and older across regions, TMREL 0.114 (0 to 0.403) to 1.87 (0.500 to 3.30), NDE 0.193 (0 to 0.900) to 6.94 (3.40 to 8.30). Global, age-standardised, both sexes: GBD 2016 0 (0 to 0.800); GBD 2016 curves with 2020 weights 0.534 (0 to 1.00), NDE 0.669 (0 to 1.40); GBD 2020 0.511 (0.400 to 0.700), NDE 1.72 (0.80 to 3.30). Hypothetical curves for alcohol use disorders and alcoholic cardiomyopathy lowered the TMREL by 0.058 to 0.146 drinks a day on average. In grams (editors' arithmetic, 10 g a drink): 0.249 drinks is about 2.5 g, 0.546 about 5.5 g, 0.511 about 5.1 g.

claims.statement: In Chinese men and in people of European descent, genetically higher alcohol intake compared with genetically lower intake is associated with more stroke, most clearly with bleeding into the brain (intracerebral haemorrhage), and the Chinese study found no sign of a lower risk at low intake; cohort studies comparing people who drink with people who do not found no overall difference in stroke but more strokes at higher intakes. No paper read gives absolute risks of stroke by amount. In 161,498 genotyped Chinese adults from ten areas, followed about 10 years, men's stroke risk rose steadily across six groups whose genotypes and area predicted mean intakes of 4 to 256 g of ethanol a week: per 100 g a week (about 14 g a day, editors' arithmetic) ischaemic stroke 1.09 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.14; 5,709 cases), intracerebral haemorrhage 1.18 (1.12 to 1.24; 2,790 cases) and all stroke 1.12 (1.09 to 1.16); the lowest group, in which two thirds did not drink, showed no sign of a raised risk, and the next two groups (about 100 g a week) had higher, not lower, risk of ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage than the three lowest groups pooled (about 25 g a week); the same genotypes showed no association in women, few of whom drink (ischaemic stroke 0.98, 0.88 to 1.09; intracerebral haemorrhage 0.96, 0.82 to 1.12); and self-reported drinking in the same men showed a U shape, with lower stroke risk at about 100 g a week than in non-drinkers and former drinkers (Millwood et al., 2019). If, and only if, there is no protective effect and the relation is log-linear, those authors estimate that alcohol caused about 8 in 100 ischaemic strokes and 16 in 100 intracerebral haemorrhages among the men studied (a model estimate). In European-descent summary data the odds of stroke were 1.27 (1.12 to 1.45) per standard deviation of genetically predicted log drinks a week, 1.21 (1.05 to 1.40) after allowing for genetic liability to smoking; ischaemic stroke 1.26 (1.09 to 1.46) and intracerebral haemorrhage 3.53 (1.70 to 7.32) (Larsson et al., 2020); in UK Biobank, a genetic score for alcohol use disorder gave 1.26 (1.04 to 1.54), not significant at that paper's threshold for six outcomes (Biddinger et al., 2022). Carriers of the ADH1B variant, who reported 17% less drinking, had lower odds of ischaemic stroke in the studies with subtype data (0.83, 0.72 to 0.95) but no difference in all stroke (0.98, 0.90 to 1.07; 10,164 strokes) (Holmes et al., 2014). In cohort studies, people who drank had, against non-drinkers (most groups including former drinkers), no different risk of new stroke (0.98, 0.91 to 1.06; 17 studies) or of stroke death (1.06, 0.91 to 1.23; 10 studies), and against lifetime abstainers a higher risk of stroke death (1.29, 1.09 to 1.53; 3 studies); by intake, new strokes were less common at up to 14.9 g a day (0.81 and 0.80; 3 studies each) and more common above 60 g a day (1.62, 1.32 to 1.98; 4 studies) (Ronksley et al., 2011); in the GBD 2016 curves ischaemic stroke dipped at low intake without statistical significance. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Millwood et al. 2019 (China Kadoorie Biobank men; genetic, per 280 g/week of genotype-predicted mean intake): ischaemic stroke RR 1.27 (1.13–1.43; 5,709 cases), intracerebral haemorrhage 1.58 (1.36–1.84; 2,790), all stroke 1.38 (1.26–1.51; 9,189); per 100 g/week 1.09 (1.04–1.14), 1.18 (1.12–1.24), 1.12 (1.09–1.16); single variants (GG against AG) stroke 1.19 (1.13–1.24) rs671 and 1.19 (1.11–1.27) rs1229984; women ischaemic stroke 0.98 (0.88–1.09), intracerebral haemorrhage 0.96 (0.82–1.12); conventional, current drinkers per 280 g/week, 1.28 (1.19–1.38), 1.59 (1.37–1.85), 1.35 (1.27–1.44), with a U shape against non-drinkers (not printed); attributable shares if there is no protection and the relation is log-linear: about 8% of ischaemic strokes and 16% of intracerebral haemorrhages in men. Larsson et al. 2020 (per SD of genetically predicted log drinks/week): stroke OR 1.27 (1.12–1.45), adjusted for smoking liability 1.21 (1.05–1.40); ischaemic stroke 1.26 (1.09–1.46); intracerebral haemorrhage 3.53 (1.70–7.32); subarachnoid haemorrhage (UK Biobank) 2.47 (1.08–5.62); ADH1B variant alone ischaemic stroke 1.31 (1.05–1.65), intracerebral haemorrhage 11.5 (1.31–101.46). Biddinger et al. 2022: stroke 1.26 (1.04–1.54; P = .021, threshold P < .008). Holmes et al. 2014 (intake-lowering variant): all stroke 0.98 (0.90–1.07), ischaemic stroke 0.83 (0.72–0.95). Ronksley et al. 2011 (cohorts; against non-drinkers, mostly current): incident stroke 0.98 (0.91–1.06), stroke death 1.06 (0.91–1.23); against lifetime abstainers 0.93 (0.85–1.02) and 1.29 (1.09–1.53); incident stroke by intake (under 2.5 to over 60 g/day) 0.81, 0.80, 0.92, 1.15, 1.62 (1.32–1.98); haemorrhagic 1.14 (0.97–1.34), ischaemic 0.92 (0.85–1.00). No absolute risks in any paper read.
